tldr: By correcting VR-recorded human roofing demonstrations against a 3D roof mesh using trajectory optimization and reinforcement learning, researchers enabled a compact humanoid (Unitree G1) to safely perform tasks from slope locomotion to stooped tool operation.
hero_caption: Overall framework for learning humanoid roofing skills. Human work demonstrations captured via VR are retargeted to the humanoid, optimized against the roof mesh, trained through reinforcement learning in Isaac Lab, and finally deployed to a physical Unitree G1.
overview:
Working on pitched roofs involves an extremely high risk of falling, making it one of the most hazardous and physically demanding jobs in construction. Prior roofing robots have mainly targeted inspection or single-function automation. However, actual job sites are designed around human body dimensions and movements. Humanoids capable of seamlessly switching between locomotion and low-posture work are therefore promising candidates.

Yet, standard walking controllers cannot be applied directly to roofs. On a slope, minor posture disturbances lead directly to falls. Furthermore, when human demonstrations recorded via VR are retargeted to the robot's kinematic skeleton, geometric mismatches inevitably arise—feet penetrate the roof surface, or hands float too far from the target work plane. Simply translating the robot's root link cannot satisfy both foot support and end-effector work relations at the same time.

To solve this, the authors propose a "scene-grounded" learning framework that uses an accurate 3D roof mesh as a spatial reference, combining trajectory-level optimization with execution-aware reinforcement learning rewards. Trajectory optimization first reconciles stable foot contact and work clearance geometrically. Then, task-semantic clearance and mesh nonpenetration rewards conditioned on work phases are added during reinforcement learning. This preserves critical work relations even when dynamic tracking errors occur.

In simulation experiments covering nailgun, hammering, and pushing motions, the policy kept work-clearance errors down to about 0.25–0.53 cm and eliminated hand mesh penetration entirely. Furthermore, zero-shot transfer to a physical Unitree G1 reproduced uphill walking and stooped tool-readiness motions on an inclined platform with mean base-frame errors below 80 mm.
contributions: Built an end-to-end pipeline that transforms VR-captured human roofing demonstrations into geometrically consistent humanoid reference trajectories grounded in roof geometry.
Developed a trajectory-level reference motion optimization method that jointly solves multi-point foot support anchors, tool work clearance, full-body mesh nonpenetration, and temporal smoothness.
Introduced phase-gated task-semantic clearance and nonpenetration rewards in reinforcement learning to preserve hand-roof spatial relations and prevent penetration despite dynamic tracking errors.

sections.heading: Why Humanoids for Roofing, and What Makes It Hard?
sections.summary: Roofing presents an extremely dangerous work environment due to heights and slopes, driving a strong need for automation. While humanoids fit well into human-oriented roof environments, directly retargeting VR demonstrations causes feet and hands to misalign with the roof mesh.
sections.details:
Roofing is among the construction sectors with the highest fatality and injury rates. Workers must handle heavy manual tasks involving physical contact, such as hauling materials and nailing, across steep, unstable footing and harsh conditions like extreme heat and wind. While wheeled and tracked robots excel at inspection or cleaning, and quadrupeds offer stable locomotion, they struggle to use human hand tools or adopt flexible low working postures like stooping and kneeling in tight roof spaces. Humanoid robots, sharing the human kinematic form, offer a promising path forward.

Operating a humanoid on a pitched roof, however, presents substantial challenges. On a slope, any change in posture disrupts balance; interaction forces from hand tools or foot placement can easily trigger a fall. An even bigger issue is the geometric mismatch that occurs when human motion data captured via VR trackers is retargeted to the robot's skeleton. VR tracking captures general motion profiles and timing, but it cannot guarantee millimeter-level spatial relations between the robot and the roof mesh. Consequently, feet sink into the roof, hands hover too far from the work surface, or hands clip through the roof. A simple rigid offset, such as lifting the root link, cannot independently correct both foot contact and hand position.

To address this, the authors propose a framework evaluated on a Unitree G1 that spatially grounds human demonstrations using a measured roof mesh, paired with dynamic reinforcement learning to absorb tracking errors. The goal is to acquire slope-adaptive whole-body locomotion that seamlessly unifies slope transit, transitions into low postures, and representative tool operations.

captions.F2: The overarching roofing construction workflow alongside the focused scope of this paper. Rather than full automation or material handling, this study concentrates on a motion-centric subset: slope transit, working-posture transitions, and representative tool/material manipulations.

sections.heading: Prior Art and the Missing Link
sections.summary: Research has advanced across visual roof inspection, dedicated machinery, rough-terrain humanoid locomotion, and motion imitation. However, no prior work has simultaneously satisfied foot contact stability on slopes and non-contact end-effector work clearance against the roof surface.
sections.details:
Prior work relevant to this paper falls into four main areas:

### Roof Perception, Inspection Robots, and Slope Locomotion
Numerous studies use aerial images from drones and UAVs for roof segmentation and damage detection. Physical roof inspection platforms, including hexapods and multi-sensor systems like Roofus, have also been developed. However, these systems aim to gather inspection data safely and do not address whole-body manipulation in stooped or kneeling postures like a roofer.

### Roofing Work Automation
Existing approaches include drone-mounted nailguns for fixing slates and teleoperated robots for asbestos roof dismantling. Yet, these are single-function, specialized machines that lack the humanoid versatility to walk to a spot, lower their posture, and carry out sequential tasks autonomously.

### Humanoid Locomotion Control
Humanoid locomotion has advanced rapidly, from MPC-based rough-terrain walking on Atlas to RL-driven robust locomotion (such as DWL), vision-based parkour, and BeamDojo, which enforces strict foot contact constraints. However, conventional locomotion primarily optimizes mobility, overlooking precise relative spatial positioning between end-effectors and work surfaces on slopes.

### Human-to-Humanoid Retargeting and Motion Tracking
Imitation frameworks like DeepMimic, PHC, OmniH2O, and BeyondMimic have matured significantly. Nonetheless, roofing requires maintaining task semantics tightly coupled to the environment mesh—such as keeping hand-to-roof distance within millimeters during designated work phases while keeping feet anchored on a pitch—which standard retargeting cannot achieve.

sections.heading: A Two-Stage Approach: Grounding Demonstrations and Dynamic Tracking
sections.summary: After retargeting VR demonstrations to the G1, trajectory optimization resolves foot contact, hand clearance, and collision avoidance against the roof mesh. In Isaac Lab, reinforcement learning with phase-gated rewards then trains the policy to suppress dynamic tracking errors.
sections.details:
The proposed architecture features a two-stage design: geometric grounding of reference trajectories via offline optimization, followed by dynamic grounding via reinforcement learning.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation
Beyond matching reference poses, the robot must maintain foot support, satisfy hand work clearance $d_w$, and avoid full-body mesh penetrations. The state space includes joint states, reference motions, and base angular velocity; actions are target position offsets for the 29 degrees of freedom.

### 3.2 Human Demonstration Collection
On a variable-pitch platform ($9^{\circ}$, $17^{\circ}$, $25^{\circ}$), nine motion categories (uphill, downhill, lateral walking, turning, stooping, kneeling, hammering, nailing, and pushing) were recorded using a Pico VR headset, hand controllers, and ankle trackers. Data was resampled from native VR rates (~72–90 Hz) down to 30 Hz.

### 3.3 Kinematic Retargeting to the Humanoid
Key joints are extracted from the 24-joint human skeleton and mapped to the 29-DOF Unitree G1 through inverse kinematics (IK) using the General Motion Retargeting (GMR) framework.

### 3.4 Task-Semantic Scene-Grounded Reference Optimization
Because raw retargeted motions $\bar{\mathcal{M}}$ misalign with the roof mesh $\mathcal{G}$, the entire trajectory is optimized:
- **Roof Frame Alignment**: A rigid transformation is computed using physical measurements, such as toe-to-roof-edge distance.
- **Support Contact Inference and Multi-Point Anchoring**: Contact phases are detected from sole-center velocity and acceleration, and five anchor points per foot are snapped to the roof surface to prevent toe penetration caused by single-ankle alignment.
- **Work Clearance**: During active tool manipulation phases ($c^{\mathrm{work}}_t=1$), hand positions are adjusted along the roof surface normal to match target clearance $d_w$ (25 cm for nailgun, 12 cm for hammering, 18.5 cm for pushing).
- **Nonpenetration and Planned Knee Contact**: Penalties prevent hand and knee collision-hull vertices from dipping below the roof mesh, while planned knee contacts are permitted during designated kneeling phases.
- **Trajectory Optimization**: Solving for joint angle adjustments $\delta\mathbf{q}_t$ and root normal adjustments $\delta r_{n,t}$, the optimization produces a smooth reference trajectory $\mathcal{M}^*$ while penalizing deviation from the original demonstration and minimizing joint accelerations.

### 3.5 Reinforcement Learning in Simulation
Using the optimized trajectories, an asymmetric Actor-Critic (PPO) policy is trained in Isaac Lab. The Actor observes reference motions, proprioception, observation history, and noisy depth images. The Critic receives privileged data, including absolute link positions and height scans. In addition to standard tracking rewards, phase-gated hand clearance rewards $r^{\mathrm{clear}}_t$ and mesh penetration penalties $c^{\mathrm{pen}}_t$ are added to keep work relations intact under dynamic lag and disturbances.

sections.heading: Rigorous Ablations in Sim and Validation on the Physical G1
sections.summary: A 5-way nailgun ablation confirmed that both reference trajectory grounding and execution-aware rewards are indispensable. The policy transferred zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1, reproducing motions with mean base-frame errors under 80 mm.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Training ran in Isaac Lab across 4,096 parallel environments. Evaluation metrics included base-frame mean per-joint position error ($\mathrm{MPJPE}_b$), foot contact error $E_{\mathrm{foot}}$, work clearance error $E_{\mathrm{work}}$, and minimum hand-mesh distance $d_{\mathrm{handmesh}}$.

### 4.2 Simulation Results: Motion and Pitch Coverage
Across the full motion library (Table 1), base-frame tracking errors for transit motions remained low, between 18.35 and 37.07 mm. In pitch coverage tests (Table 2), a policy trained only on $9^{\circ}+17^{\circ}$ fell on an unseen $25^{\circ}$ pitch, yielding a 0% completion rate. Adding $25^{\circ}$ data enabled 100% completion across all pitches, indicating that depth sensing alone cannot extrapolate to steep slopes without explicit pitch demonstrations.

### 4.3 Nailgun Ablation Study (A/M/B/C/D)
The core ablation evaluated five variants across three seeds (Table 3):
- **A (Raw retargeting)**: Hand penetrated the roof by over 10 cm, failing.
- **M (Global uniform offset) / B (Foot contact grounding)**: Foot errors improved, but neglecting hand constraints left ~14 cm clearance errors and hand penetration.
- **C (Reference task optimization)**: Even with perfect reference targets, dynamic policy lag caused hands to hover at 32.86 cm on average instead of the target 25 cm (an error of ~7.8 cm).
- **D (Proposed: adding execution-aware task rewards)**: Hand clearance error dropped sharply to $0.531\pm 0.104$ cm with zero hand penetration (minimum distance $+0.165$ cm), succeeding across all three seeds.

### 4.4 Cross-Task Evaluations and Baselines
For hammering (12 cm target) and pushing (18.5 cm target), variant C suffered ~1.7 cm hand penetration, whereas proposed variant D eliminated penetration and kept clearance errors to 0.256 cm and 0.424 cm, respectively (Table 4).
In contrast, "pure RL" without motion priors collapsed into an unnatural, overly crouched posture, achieving only a 6% task success rate. Zero-shot teleoperation (SONIC) failed immediately in both trials as the robot lost balance stepping onto the pitched platform.

### 4.5 Real-Robot Evaluation
The Unitree G1 was deployed on an ~$11.8^{\circ}$ inclined foam mat with a safety hoist (Table 6). Over five trials per motion, base-frame tracking error $\mathrm{MPJPE}_b$ remained under 80 mm across the board: $60.2\pm 0.8$ mm for nailgun, $79.9\pm 3.1$ mm for hammering, $61.4\pm 1.6$ mm for stooping, and $27.6$ mm for uphill walking. Joint error analysis revealed that lower-body tracking (RMSE ~$9.4^{\circ}$, ankle error ~87 mm) had larger errors than the upper body (RMSE ~$5.0^{\circ}$), highlighting slope contact adaptation as the primary physical tracking challenge.

sections.heading: Takeaways, Construction Relevance, and Current Limitations
sections.summary: Results confirm that grounding human demonstrations to the environmental mesh is essential. Formulating construction tasks around spatial clearances rather than joint tracking provides high engineering value, though rough roof surfaces and real-world force control remain future challenges.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Interpretation of Results
The primary takeaway is that human-like motion imitation and environmental mesh grounding are separate challenges that must be explicitly bridged. Fixing foot contact alone breaks hand positioning, and fixing reference hand poses still results in hand floating or penetration due to dynamic tracking lag in RL. Combining trajectory optimization with execution-aware rewards is essential to achieve millimeter-level clearance.

### 5.2 Implications for Construction Robotics
Construction work is defined less by pure transit and more by spatial geometric relations—maintaining specific tool distances and angles relative to the work surface. Combining low-cost wearable VR tracking of skilled tradespeople with precise mesh models from BIM or 3D scans offers a practical path for programming future construction humanoids.

### 5.3 Limitations and Next Steps
- **Simplified Roof Models**: Experiments used flat wooden and foam slopes, leaving unmodeled real-world disturbances like overlapping slate shingles, surface roughness, debris, and wind or rain.
- **Hand Clearance Formulation**: The setup evaluates geometric clearance without tool collision hulls, nailgun contact reaction forces, or hammer impact dynamics.
- **Hardware Constraints**: The physical robot operated under a safety hoist, whose slight tension may have aided balance recovery. Without an external MoCap system, absolute spatial distances between hand and roof could not be measured as rigorously as in simulation.

sections.heading: Toward Construction Humanoids via Grounded Skilled Demonstrations
sections.summary: Scene-grounded learning, which aligns human demonstrations with the environment mesh, enables humanoids to combine stable slope walking with precise working postures. This marks a solid step toward whole-body motion primitives for construction sites.
sections.details:
This study presented a framework for humanoid robots to learn adaptive whole-body motions from human demonstrations in hazardous pitched-roof construction environments.

To overcome foot floating and hand collision issues inherent in direct kinematic retargeting, the approach combines multi-point support anchoring and task clearance optimization against a 3D roof mesh with phase-gated execution-aware RL rewards. This kept work clearance errors for nailing and hammering within millimeter levels (0.25–0.53 cm). Furthermore, physical experiments on a Unitree G1 confirmed that simulation-trained policies transfer directly to real hardware.

These findings suggest that scene-grounded demonstration learning serves as a viable foundation for humanoids to adapt to human tools and spaces, unlocking new possibilities for construction automation.

takeaways: Directly retargeting human demonstrations to humanoids causes geometric mismatches with the environment mesh; trajectory optimization that independently resolves multi-point foot contact and hand clearance is essential.

Even with a geometrically corrected reference trajectory, dynamic tracking lag causes hands to drift from the work surface; reinforcement learning rewards must include task-phase-gated clearance and nonpenetration terms.
Depth observations alone cannot extrapolate humanoid balance to unseen steep slopes zero-shot, making it crucial to include the target slope range in the training dataset.
limitations: Evaluations were restricted to flat planar slope meshes, omitting real-world roofing complexities like shingle steps, surface roughness, debris, and wet conditions.
Physical tool and material dynamics were omitted in favor of palm-center clearances, leaving heavy contact force control (such as hammering impacts or nailing recoil) unaddressed.
Physical testing used a safety hoist and lacked external motion capture, preventing complete verification of untethered fall rates and absolute spatial task accuracy in the real world.
